en: Oṃ, homage to the Buddha!
I perpetually pay homage to the All-Knowing One, who is free from conceptual proliferation, without objective support, inconceivable, unchanging, and liberated from all defects.
I pay homage to that best of speakers, by whose grace the mass of darkness of delusion is clearly destroyed, and who perceives the true nature of the world.

[2] Here, indeed, a bodhisattva who desires to fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). In that regard, first of all, having sat upon a comfortable seat in some secluded place agreeable to the mind, and having assumed the cross-legged posture (*paryaṅka*), one should observe these beings of the six realms of existence as suffering through the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*pariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); then, endowed with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one should generate the thought of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

[3] Thereafter, in order to ascertain the true nature of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), to make it firm, and to lead it to growth, development, expansion, and fulfillment, one should contemplate phenomena in this way: That which appears in the form of blue, yellow, and so forth, is neither an external nor an internal entity, because it is devoid of a nature that is either unitary or manifold. To explain: it is not unitary, because it appears with distinct parts; nor is it manifold, because it cannot be established as consisting of atoms, since the atom itself is untenable.

For instance, if it were to have parts, how could it be an atom? If, on the other hand, it were partless, then atoms joined together would occupy no space distinct from one another because they would be conjoined in their entirety; thus, every aggregate would be a mere atom—a single elephant, a mountain, and even the ocean [would be so]. And it is said in the *Āryalaṅkāvatāra*: "No external object exists in the way it is conceptualized by the foolish;
the mind, stirred by latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), proceeds appearing as objects."
"Just as a form is seen in a mirror, free from being either identical to or different [from it], yet does not exist there, so too is the nature of things within all phenomena."

Therefore, there is no object of apprehension external to consciousness. Due to the absence of that [object], the state of being an apprehender also does not exist for consciousness. In every respect, the duality of the apprehended and the apprehender does not exist; thus says the proponent of consciousness (*vijñānavādin*). And this has been stated with reference to the imagined (*parikalpita*) consciousness.

[4] Consequently, for fools whose intellects are overwhelmed by the power of the habitual tendencies of beginningless ignorance, that very object appears in various non-existent forms. Taking that very non-existent form as a causal sign (*nimitta*), the world’s conceptualization of duality and its grasping at duality—which serve as the source of all misfortune—proceeds. As long as this form appears, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is not seen, just as those with ophthalmia who perceive hairs, mosquitoes, and so forth do not see the emptiness of those hairs and the like.

[5] Then, having thus investigated, he completely abandons all names and all signs. Thereupon, for him who abides in the non-conceptual, signless samādhi that takes no objective support (anālambana) regarding all phenomena, there arises—through the power of the impressions of previous practice, effortlessly and without volitional construction—a supramundane cognition that is non-conceptual, signless, a vision of the emptiness of all phenomena, resembling the solitary, stainless, and infinite sky. This occurs because all signs of conceptual proliferation have set.

[6] That alone is the ultimate bodhicitta; that alone is the primary *prajñāpāramitā*; and that alone is the path that serves as the antidote to all obscurations. By means of that antidote, through the total exhaustion of all seeds of afflicted phenomena and their latencies residing within the *ālayavijñāna*, and through the cessation of those consciousnesses that manifest as the basis, body, and objects of enjoyment, that *ālayavijñāna* abandons the characteristics of the *ālayavijñāna* and assumes the characteristics of the untainted realm (*anāsravadhātu*).

[7] That very same is the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*); it is the *dharma-kāya* of the Buddhas; the limit of reality (*bhūta-koṭi*); suchness (*tathatā*); the ultimate object (*paramārtha*); and the realm of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*). It is called the "limit of reality" because it is the limit (*koṭi*)—the boundary—of realities (*bhūta*), that is, of true principles (*tattva*). It is called "suchness" because it exists eternally in just that way. It is the "ultimate object" because it is the object (*artha*) of the supreme (*parama*) supramundane knowledge; or, it is the ultimate and it is an object, thus it is the ultimate object. It is the "realm of phenomena" because it is the realm (*dhātu*), the support, of phenomena (*dharma*), which here refers to the noble qualities (*āryadharma*).

Upon its attainment, the attainment of the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) and the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), which are characterized by the welfare of the entire world in all its aspects, depends upon it.
[8] Thus, these stages arise for one who cultivates this Blessed Perfection of Wisdom, as it has been said in the *Ālokamālā* (vv. 251–253):
"One becomes as if indifferent, as if sleeping, and devoid of longing."
Having taken as its object the selflessness of the mind, the weary mind finds, as it were, rest.
Emptiness causes stiffness of the eyes and bowing of the head,
as well as the numbness of the mind and mental factors for those who perceive emptiness.
Thinking "I have seen reality and my purpose is fulfilled," the hero should not abandon his meditative cultivation because of observing signs; for even beyond this, there is that which is supreme.
For example:
"Because this imagined [nature] has been discarded, it is like a painting from which something has been erased. (Ālokamālā 236–238)
Even when arisen from meditation, he beholds the entire world as gloomy.
Like something decayed, withered, and broken on all sides;
like a deserted village, ruined, without pleasure groves, and without refuge.
Producing intense agitation like the cry of a cricket,
it was ownerless, devoid of wealth, and nothing more than a mere name.
Thus ends the definition of the negation of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Furthermore, Kambalāmbarapāda says:
"But when the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has been perceived, one then perceives..."
Mounted upon the flow of one's own mind, it seems as if it enters within oneself.
That very thing, appearing like a magical illusion, is nothing but a mere delusion;
not seeing it there as it is imagined, one perceives it as if overcome by darkness.
It is as if permeated on all sides by the lines of residual impressions (*vāsanā*),
as if crowded with afflictions (*kleśa*), and as if revolving like a wheel.
Knowledge arising from deep sleep is both the object and the subject, as well as the defining characteristic;
it is like something seen and then lost—what indeed does it perceive?
Thus is the characteristic of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Furthermore, they themselves say:
"In perfected cognition (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), however, everything has a single flavor."
It is undivided, without beginning or end, formless, and free from grasping.
Without elevation, without depression, neither long nor circular,
it is stainless like the sky when its darkness has been pierced by the sun.
Through the penetration of the dharma of equality, everything is again entirely equal;
by way of conventional truth, this is the seen dharma, yet it is not perceived in the ultimate sense.
Conceptual construction is known as the conventional truth, the cause of further conceptual constructions;
that very same [reality], however, is the ultimate truth, which brings conceptual construction to an end.
Such is the extensive detail. The bliss of supramundane perfection is ineffable; because it cannot be expressed and is to be personally realized within oneself, it is not described.

[9] Furthermore, one who cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*) should recognize six thieves who, having plundered the wealth of wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*), cause one to fall into misfortune. They are as follows: lethargy and drowsiness (*styāna-middha*), laxity and excitement (*laya-auddhatya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). Among these, lethargy (*styāna*) is a specific state such as heaviness of the body produced by eating curd and the like. Drowsiness (*middha*) is simply sleep. Laxity (*laya*) is a sinking of the mind, a lack of clarity in its activity toward the object of focus (*ālambana*). Excitement (*auddhatya*) is a restlessness of the mind, a state of distraction.
*Kaukṛtya* is that which is done badly (*kukṛta*); its state is *kaukṛtya*, a specific form of remorse. *Vicikitsā* is doubt: "Is what was taught by the teacher thus, or not?"

[10] In that regard, for the pacification of lethargy and drowsiness (*styāna-middha*), one should practice moderation in food, mindfulness of impermanence (*anityatā-smaraṇa*), and the contemplation of autumn, a hundred years, or a hundred leagues. For the removal of laxity (*laya*), one should cultivate the power of wisdom and vigor, or recollect things that inspire joy, such as gardens, ponds, autumn, and moonlight. Through the pacification of restlessness (*auddhatya*), there is tranquility (*upaśama*). For the destruction of remorse and doubt (*kaukṛtya-vicikitsā*), one should recollect the qualities of meditative concentration (*samādhi-guṇa*). Furthermore, one should have intense faith, respect, affection, and serene confidence toward spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
And when the mind becomes free from the six faults and flows spontaneously, then one should maintain equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward that which has correctly proceeded.
[11] Having emerged from meditative concentration, one should make a formal aspiration.
Without experiencing the suffering of the miserable realms and without the practice of difficult austerities,
may the world attain Buddhahood with a single divine body.
Or one should recite the *Bhadracaryā* and other such prayers of aspiration.
The *Prajñāpāramitābhāvanākrama* is completed.
This work is by the venerable Ratnākaraśānti, the Great Scholar of Pūrva-deśa and the Omniscient One of the Kali Age.
